I'm not much of a reader, I'll admit that, but recently I've been getting the urge to expand my mind a bit. I think reading is one of the best ways to expand your horizons and learn new things but I don't know enough about literature to know where to begin. Id like to read something by a famous author, something read by most literature enthusiasts that I can discuss with average people here and IRL. Something like Hemingway, but I'm afraid I wont have the attention span if his other stuff is anything like the old man and the sea, which I read in HS.

Any suggestions for a gripping fiction books that will make me really think/grow as a person?

Some things I've read (a long time ago) include:

Old Man and the Sea, Of Mice and Men (which i think is kind of what i'm looking for, human condition or something of the like), Grapes of Wrath, and To Kill a Mockingbird

Edit : Formatted better

The Angel's Game by Carlos Ruiz Zafon. It's sort of a prequel to The Shadow of The Wind, but you 100% do not need to read it if you want to read The Angel's Game. There are a plethora of ideas presented in the book, and while some may seem cynical, they are contrasted in many different ways, with a variety of characters present.

I'm going to base my recommendations off of two factors. 1. The book is a satisfactory introductory novel for those looking to get into reading literature. 2. The book is popular, and therefore you will likely meet people who have read it.

  • 1984 - George Orwell
  • Slaughterhouse-Five Kurt Vonnegut
  • A Farewell to Arms - Hemingway (I know you said you're wary of his writing, but you also said you want something that touches upon the human condition. I'm not exaggerating when I say this book has the power to rip your heart out if you give it the chance. It is the saddest book I've read, and if you have ever watched Silver Linings Playbook, this is the book that the main character chucks out the window at the beginning.)
  • Labyrinths - Jorge Luis Borges (This isn't a novel, but rather a collection of short stories that are redolent with an intelligence, wealth of invention and a tight, almost mathematically formal style that challenge with mysteries and paradoxes revealed only after several readings. I recommend this to people that are uncertain that they can commit to a full novel. I have yet to hear a bad review of this work; it's simply mind-blowing.)
  • Norwegian Wood - Haruki Murakami (Murakami's work is a little... strange. There will be times that you might cringe at what the characters are doing, and the fact that they do it in such a nonchalant way. However, he also has this very strange, intimate way of writing that will make you feel like his voice is reverberating within the depths of your very soul. Norwegian Wood is his most realist novel, but he has made a name for himself by writing magic-surrealism [think strange, dark, dreamlike stuff, not Harry Potter or literal magic]. If you want to give his surreal writing a shot, take a look at Kafka on the Shore.)
  • Metamorphosis - Franz Kafka (A popular novella)
  • L'Etranger (The Stranger) - Albert Camus (Another short novel)

Note: I also would like to take the moment to address a common pitfall that affects many that are interested in literature, and I'm going to make it brief. Give audiobooks a shot. They are no worse or better than reading unless the author has used the physical words on a page to create images or convey some sort of message beyond their oratory message. The only example of this that I can think of (excluding poetry) would be House of Leaves, where passages are written backwards, have to be read in a mirror, or form images that further immerse the reader. And for the love of god, enjoy what you read. There's no need to power through a dull book simply to say you've read it. There are so many great works out there, waiting to be enjoyed. Seek them out. Also, don't forget to share your experiences with us!
